content: A biased sample refers to a statistical sample of a population in which certain members of the population are less likely to be included than others. In extreme cases, some members of the population may be entirely excluded from the sample, meaning they have zero probability of being selected. For instance, a survey conducted among high school students to assess teenage illegal drug use would be considered biased because it excludes homeschooled students and dropouts. Similarly, a sample is biased if certain groups are either underrepresented or overrepresented compared to others in the population. For example, a man on the street interview conducted at a specific location would likely overrepresent healthy individuals who are more likely to be out and about, while underrepresenting those with chronic illnesses who are less likely to leave their homes. A biased sample introduces significant problems because any statistical conclusions drawn from it are prone to consistent errors. This bias can result in either an overestimation or underestimation of the corresponding parameter in the population. In practice, nearly all samples are biased to some degree, as achieving a perfectly random sample is virtually impossible. However, if the degree of underrepresentation is minimal, the sample can still serve as a reasonable approximation of a random sample. Additionally, if the underrepresented group does not differ significantly from other groups in the variable being measured, the sample may still provide a reasonable approximation. It is important to note that while the term bias often carries a negative connotation implying intentional deception, in statistical contexts, it refers to a mathematical property. While some individuals may deliberately use biased samples to produce misleading results, more often, biased samples arise from the inherent challenges of obtaining a truly representative sample. In some cases, sampling designs are intentionally biased. For example, the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) deliberately oversamples minority populations in its nationwide surveys to ensure sufficient precision for estimates within these groups. These surveys require the use of sample weights to produce accurate estimates across all racial and ethnic groups. Examples of biased samples include online and phone-in polls, which are inherently biased because respondents are self-selected. Individuals who are highly motivated to respond, often those with strong opinions, are overrepresented, while those who are indifferent or apathetic are less likely to participate. This often results in polarized responses, with extreme perspectives receiving disproportionate weight in the summary, rendering such polls unscientific. A classic example of a biased sample occurred during the 1936 U.S. presidential election when the Literary Digest predicted that Alf Landon would defeat Franklin Roosevelt by a large margin. The opposite result occurred. The survey's sample was drawn from magazine readers, automobile owners, and telephone users, which overrepresented wealthy individuals who were more likely to vote Republican. In contrast, a smaller poll of 50,000 citizens conducted by George Gallup's organization accurately predicted the election outcome, leading to the rise of the Gallup poll. Another example occurred during the 1948 U.S. presidential election when the Chicago Tribune mistakenly printed the headline Dewey Defeats Truman. This error was based on a phone survey, which was not representative of the general population at the time, as telephone ownership was limited to wealthier individuals with stable addresses. Additionally, the Gallup poll the Tribune relied on was over two weeks old at the time of printing. When entire segments of a population are excluded from a sample, no statistical adjustments can make the estimates representative of the entire population. However, if certain groups are underrepresented and the degree of underrepresentation can be quantified, sample weights can be used to correct the bias. For example, in a hypothetical population of 10 million men and 10 million women, a biased sample of 100 individuals that includes 20 men and 80 women could be adjusted by assigning a weight of 2.5 to each man and 0.625 to each woman. This adjustment would ensure that the estimates reflect the same expected values as a sample with equal representation of men and women. The spotlight fallacy occurs when someone assumes that all members of a group or category share the characteristics of those who receive the most media attention. This fallacy follows the reasoning: (1) Members of group X with quality Q receive significant media attention, and (2) therefore, all members of group X possess quality Q. This reasoning is flawed because the fact that certain individuals or events attract media attention does not mean they are representative of the entire group. For example, if a mass murderer from a small town receives extensive media coverage, it would be incorrect to conclude that everyone from that town is a mass murderer. The spotlight fallacy derives its name from the idea that receiving significant attention is akin to being in the spotlight. It is similar to other fallacies, such as hasty generalization, biased sampling, and misleading vividness, as it involves generalizing about a population based on an inadequate or flawed sample. This fallacy is particularly common when people assume that those who receive the most media attention represent the groups they belong to. For instance, some individuals may believe that all opponents of abortion are willing to commit acts of violence against doctors simply because such incidents receive significant media coverage. Since the media typically focuses on unusual or exceptional events, it is illogical to assume that these events are representative of the broader population. Examples of the Spotlight Fallacy: I wouldn’t like to go to America because of all the gun crime; we see it on the news all the time. Muslims are always in the news blowing people up; so all Muslims must be terrorists. A doctor might say, Why don’t patients make an effort to look after themselves? My surgery is full of people who eat, drink, smoke, and don’t exercise. However, the doctor may have many more patients who do take care of themselves and rarely visit the surgery. Why do young people all take drugs and mug old ladies? You read about it in the paper all the time. A child might say, When I grow up, I want to be a singer, based on the disproportionate media attention given to singers.
